questions.q: In SOC terms, what does Owen say "done" looks like?
options: Seeing a sign-in, a firewall allow, and a Linux auth event from the same window of time, side by side
questions.explain: Owen cares about real, correlated visibility across sources instead of checking three separate systems by hand.

questions.q: In audit terms, what does Renee say "done" looks like?
options: Being able to show, months later, exactly what's watched, what catches what, who can access what, and what the team does when something fires
questions.explain: Renee cares about documented, repeatable process she could show an auditor -- not the underlying query syntax.

questions.q: What is Mara's actual job in reconciling the two asks?
options: Pick Owen's answer and ignore Renee's
Notice that a single, well-built SOC produces both outcomes at once, without either stakeholder compromising
Ask Owen and Renee to resolve it between themselves
questions.explain: Neither stakeholder needs to compromise if the project is scoped so the same deliverables serve both goals.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four concrete deliverables this project scopes?
questions.explain: The four deliverables are multi-source ingestion, a cross-source correlation rule, a Conditional Access pilot, and an incident-response runbook -- not a ticketing system.

questions.q: Why does this scoping conversation need to happen before any connector setup or rule-writing begins?
options: It doesn't matter when it happens
Skipping it risks building something technically impressive that satisfies one stakeholder and fails the other
Owen and Renee require a signed contract first
Sentinel requires a written scope document to be configured at all
questions.explain: Naming the deliverables with both stakeholders in the room up front keeps every later lesson pointed at a goal both people actually need.
